topicTitle: Haloacids (HCl, HBr and HI): comparative study on preparation, properties (reducing strength, acidic nature and solubility) and uses
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — One Family, Three Personalities

HCl, HBr and HI: same formula shape, steeply different behaviour. This topic compares their preparation, properties, reducing strength, acidic nature and solubility — and explains every trend from the bond.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Preparation

- **HCl (lab):** NaCl + conc. H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HCl (below 200 °C; dry gas, upward delivery — heavier than air). Industrial: burning H₂ in Cl₂ (synthesis), or by-product of chlorination.
- **HBr:** cannot use conc. H₂SO₄ (it oxidises Br⁻ to Br₂); use **KBr + conc. H₃PO₄** instead: KBr + H₃PO₄ → KH₂PO₄ + HBr.
- **HI:** same problem, worse; use **KI + conc. H₃PO₄** → KH₂PO₄ + HI. Or hydrolysis of PBr₃/PI₃: PBr₃ + 3H₂O → H₃PO₃ + 3HBr.

### 2.2 Comparative properties

| Property | HCl | HBr | HI | Trend |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bond length | 127 pm | 141 pm | 161 pm | increases |
| Bond energy | 431 | 366 | 299 kJ/mol | decreases |
| Thermal stability | most | less | least (decomposes: 2HI → H₂ + I₂) | decreases |
| Reducing strength | weak | stronger | strongest (reduces H₂SO₄ → SO₂/S, oxidised to I₂) | increases |
| Acidic strength | strong | stronger | strongest | increases |
| Boiling point | −85 °C | −67 °C | −35 °C | increases (but HCl lowest — HF anomaly excluded) |
| Fuming in moist air | yes (white fumes) | yes | yes | all form acidic mist |

### 2.3 The two opposing trends

- **Acidity and reducing power increase** down the group (bond weakens, H–X breaks easier, X⁻ bigger and more polarisable).
- **Thermal stability decreases** down the group for the same reason.
- HI reduces even conc. H₂SO₄: 2HI + H₂SO₄ → I₂ + SO₂ + 2H₂O — which is exactly why H₂SO₄ cannot be used to make it.

### 2.4 Uses

- **HCl:** gastric juice (digestion, pH 1.5–3.5), metal pickling (descaling), chlorination, lab reagent, making Cl₂/MnCl₂.
- **HBr:** ethylene dibromide (historical petrol additive), AgBr emulsions, alkyl bromides in organic synthesis.
- **HI:** reducing agent in organic chemistry, iodide salts, hydriodic acid for iodometry.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Hydrogen halide** | Binary compound of H and a halogen | HCl, HBr, HI |
| **Reducing strength** | Ease of halide ion oxidation | I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ |
| **Thermal stability** | Resistance to decomposition by heat | HCl > HBr > HI |
| **Fuming** | White acidic mist in moist air | all three HX |
| **Pickling** | Acid removal of oxide scale from steel | HCl dip |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why H₂SO₄ is disqualified for HBr and HI

- Concentrated H₂SO₄ is an oxidising acid. With NaCl it merely forms HCl (Cl⁻ too weak a reducer to be oxidised further). With KBr it oxidises half the bromide to Br₂ (2KBr + 2H₂SO₄(conc) → K₂SO₄ + Br₂ + SO₂ + 2H₂O) — the gas comes out contaminated and purple. With KI it goes further, to SO₂ or even H₂S, and liberates I₂. Hence the switch to non-oxidising H₃PO₄.

### 4.2 Why acidity rises as stability falls

- Both trace to the same bond: longer, weaker H–X means easier proton release (acidity up) and easier homolysis (stability down, reducing power up). One parameter, three symptoms — the exam's favourite "explain the trend" question.

### 4.3 Verified PYQ mapping

- NEB 2024's oxoacid-strength question was answered at row 67; the halogen-vs-helium diving question (NEB 2023) is recorded at row 63. No fresh PYQ targets this row — all items NEB-style.

## 5. Comparison Tables

| Feature | HCl | HBr | HI |
|---|---|---|---|
| Prep acid | conc. H₂SO₄ | conc. H₃PO₄ | conc. H₃PO₄ |
| With conc. H₂SO₄ | stable | → Br₂ + SO₂ | → I₂ + SO₂/H₂S |
| Reducing power | +1 only... weakest | stronger | strongest |
| Reduces MnO₂ | yes (with conc.) | yes | yes |
| Test with AgNO₃ | white AgCl | cream AgBr | yellow AgI |

## 6. Common Confusions

- **"HCl is the strongest of the three because Cl is most electronegative."** Backwards — acidity increases down the group; HI is the strongest acid of the three (bond weakness beats electronegativity).
- **"HF belongs in this comparison with the same trend."** HF breaks the pattern: its H-bonding gives it a surprisingly high boiling point and, despite F's electronegativity, it is a *weak* acid in water.
- **"Boiling point rises smoothly."** For HCl–HBr–HI yes; including HF it does not — HF's hydrogen bonding is the anomaly.

## 7. Exam Application

- The H₂SO₄-vs-H₃PO₄ preparation contrast with the oxidation equations is the classic 3-mark answer.
- Quote the trend table with numbers (bond energies, boiling points) — numerical anchors score.
- Reducing strength: 2HI + H₂SO₄ → I₂ + SO₂ + 2H₂O is the proof equation.

universalFacts: Your stomach makes roughly 2 litres of 0.1 M HCl every day — the same molecule that pickles steel digests your lunch.
examples: ***The self-defeating preparation*** — try to make HI with concentrated H2SO4 and the acid oxidises its own product: the iodide reduces the sulphate to SO2 while becoming brown I2 vapour. H3PO4, too weak to oxidise anything, is the only honest choice.
practiceQuestions: **NEB-style (3m): How is hydrogen chloride prepared in the laboratory? Why is the same method not used for HI?** — **HCl:** dry sodium chloride is heated with concentrated sulphuric acid below 200 °C: **NaCl + H₂SO₄(conc) → NaHSO₄ + HCl**. The gas is dried with concentrated H₂SO₄ and collected by **upward delivery** (heavier than air). **Why not for HI:** concentrated H₂SO₄ is an oxidising acid. Chloride is too weak a reducer to be oxidised, so HCl comes through clean; but iodide is a strong reducer — **2HI + H₂SO₄ → I₂ + SO₂ + 2H₂O** — the acid destroys its own product, giving violet I₂ vapour and SO₂ contamination (with bromide the same happens to a lesser degree). Hence **KI + concentrated H₃PO₄**, a non-oxidising acid, is used instead: **KI + H₃PO₄ → KH₂PO₄ + HI**.

**NEB-style (2m): Arrange HCl, HBr and HI in order of (a) thermal stability and (b) reducing strength, with reasons.** — **(a) Stability: HCl > HBr > HI.** Bond energies fall 431 → 366 → 299 kJ/mol as the bond lengthens (127 → 141 → 161 pm); the weaker the bond, the more easily heat snaps it, so HI decomposes visibly (2HI → H₂ + I₂) while HCl is stable to red heat. **(b) Reducing strength: HI > HBr > HCl.** The same weak bond releases the halide's electrons readily: iodide is oxidised to I₂ even by conc. H₂SO₄, bromide less readily, chloride hardly at all. Both trends are one cause wearing two faces — the falling H–X bond energy down the group.

**NEB-style (2m): State two uses each of HCl and HI.** — **HCl:** (1) in **gastric juice** (pH 1.5–3.5) it activates pepsin and kills microbes in the stomach; (2) industrially it **pickles steel** — dissolving oxide scale before galvanising or rolling — and serves as the feedstock for chlorination and Cl₂ manufacture. **HI:** (1) as a **reducing agent** in organic chemistry (converting, e.g., alkyl halides back to alkanes); (2) in **iodometry**, where hydriodic acid supplies iodide for iodine-liberating titrations, and for preparing iodide salts.

Trends down group: bond length 127->141->161 pm, bond energy 431->366->299 kJ/mol, thermal stability HCl > HBr > HI, reducing strength HI > HBr > HCl, acidic strength HI > HBr > HCl, bp -85/-67/-35 C. All fume in moist air. Uses: HCl gastric juice, pickling, chlorination; HBr AgBr films, alkyl bromides; HI reducing agent, iodometry.
summary: One family, three personalities, one cause. **HCl** (bond 431 kJ/mol) is stable, the weakest reducer, and the only one clean enough to make with oxidising H₂SO₄; **HBr** (366) needs H₃PO₄ because H₂SO₄ turns half its bromide into brown Br₂; **HI** (299) is so reducing it reduces the sulphate to SO₂ while turning to violet I₂ vapour. Down the group the H–X bond lengthens (127 → 141 → 161 pm), so **thermal stability falls** (HCl > HBr > HI) while **acidity and reducing power rise** (HI > HBr > HCl) — the same weakened bond releases its proton easily and its electrons even more easily. All three fume in moist air and all three are caught by the AgX colour ladder (white, cream, yellow). Uses: HCl pickles steel and digests food at pH 1.5; HBr feeds photographic emulsions; HI reduces and titrates.
